strengths: The paper identifies a useful, underexamined capability: elementary geometric perception distinct from long-chain geometry reasoning. The six categories—existence, counting, size, location, reference, and relationships—provide a reasonably interpretable diagnostic decomposition.

GePBench is substantial in scale (80K images and 285K questions), and its procedural construction makes exact labels possible in principle. The paper evaluates a broad set of 20 closed- and open-source MLLMs, including multiple model scales.

The results expose large and informative gaps: even the strongest reported model averages only 68.4%, versus 99.3% for humans, with particularly poor size and location performance. Per-category reporting is more useful than a single aggregate score.

The downstream experiment goes beyond benchmark construction: LLaVA-GeP is compared with a separately trained LLaVA-1.5 baseline under reportedly matched training procedures, and gains are reported across general, mathematical, and chart benchmarks.

The manuscript is organized clearly, includes prompts, model/checkpoint identifiers, training hyperparameters, computational resources, a noise ablation, and a human evaluation. The synthetic data avoid obvious privacy concerns.
weaknesses: Benchmark validity is not established sufficiently for the central claims. All questions come from templates, yet there are no text-only, image-shuffling, option-position, or question-template baselines to rule out answer priors and linguistic shortcuts. The below-chance size results and the finding that added noise sometimes improves accuracy make such controls especially important.

The generator is underspecified: the complete relationship inventory, attribute ranges and sampling distributions, overlap threshold, noise parameters, distractor construction, uniqueness checks, split construction, deduplication procedure, and random seeds are absent. The code and data are only promised for future release. Consequently, neither the benchmark nor its reported scores are presently reproducible.

The use of structured descriptions as ground truth does not by itself ensure that rendered questions are visually unambiguous. For example, reference questions can admit multiple shapes satisfying a comparison; perturbing outlines can change fine relationships such as tangency; and centroid-based quadrant labels need explicit boundary handling. Five students solving a small subset with aggregate accuracy does not audit these failure modes or report agreement and error patterns by template.

The downstream evidence does not isolate geometric perception as the cause of improvement. LLaVA-GeP receives hundreds of thousands of additional image-caption and instruction examples, while no equal-data control using unrelated synthetic images, shuffled geometric supervision, or captions alone is provided. Improvements are generally small, some general benchmarks regress or remain unchanged, and there are no multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. Thus the claimed foundational role and transfer benefit are stronger than the evidence supports.

Several architectural explanations are speculative. Claims that invariance causes poor spatial perception or that additional positional embeddings cause mixed-encoder degradation are inferred from performance correlations, while the compared encoder checkpoints can differ in architecture, pretraining data, and training procedure. No controlled intervention supports these causal conclusions.

The easy/hard definition conflates shape count and the presence of noise, preventing attribution of difficulty; moreover, results sometimes improve with noise. Difficulty calibration, performance broken down by individual controlled factor, and robustness to rendering styles or genuinely real-world geometric imagery are missing, limiting external validity.

The comparison with humans and other benchmarks is not fully controlled: Figure 7 mixes GPT-4o and GPT-4V, heterogeneous metrics, selected splits, and results collected from different sources. A fixed 60% 'passing threshold' is introduced without justification. Model evaluations collected in December 2024 are also dated for an ICML 2026 assessment.

The limitations section mentions only benchmark size and incomplete model coverage, while omitting the more consequential synthetic-to-real gap, template artifacts, possible train-test overlap at the generator level, ambiguity, API version dependence, and causal limitations of the downstream study.

The human-subject discussion states that five volunteers were informed their responses would be recorded, but gives no information about compensation, institutional review/consent procedure, recruitment safeguards, or data handling. The risk is low, but the ethics reporting is incomplete.

strengths: Significance: Geometric perception is a useful and under-evaluated capability, and separating existence, counting, size, location, reference, and relationship questions provides an interpretable diagnostic framework.

Evaluation breadth: The paper reports results for many open- and closed-source MLLMs, several model scales, and multiple visual encoders; the human comparison also establishes that sampled questions are generally easy for people.

Methodology: Programmatic generation from structured scene descriptions can provide inexpensive, precisely parameterized data at substantial scale. The inclusion of noisy renderings and easy/hard subsets is potentially useful.

The LLaVA-GeP experiment is promising: adding synthetic geometric data is associated with gains on several mathematical and chart benchmarks, including relatively visible improvements on ChartBench and ChartQA.
Presentation is mostly organized and readable, and the appendix supplies model identifiers, training hyperparameters, evaluation prompts, and some human-evaluation details.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central downstream claim is not causally established. LLaVA-GeP receives roughly 300K additional pretraining examples and 240K additional instruction examples, but there is no equal-size generic-synthetic, caption-only, or unrelated-data control. The reported improvements could therefore result from additional data or optimization rather than geometric perception specifically.

Soundness: LLaVA-GeP is not evaluated on a held-out GePBench set, so the paper never demonstrates that the intervention actually improves the targeted capability. There are also no multiple training runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests; many downstream changes are small.

Benchmark validity is insufficiently audited. Figure 1 contains an explicit answer-label inconsistency: “circumscribed” is option C, while the displayed answer says “B. circumscribed.” Ground truth is inherited from latent descriptions, but the paper does not quantify whether rendering, overlap filtering, clipping, rasterization, or added noise preserves visually observable relations and measurements.

No text-only, image-shuffling, answer-frequency, or simple computer-vision baselines are reported. Consequently, template and option-position artifacts are unmeasured, and it is unclear how much performance reflects visual geometric perception rather than dataset regularities. The construction and human study also do not establish quality across all 285K questions.

The easy/hard definition conflates shape count and the presence of noise rather than isolating difficulty factors. More shapes can simultaneously change distractors, occlusion, and relationship distributions. Exact tangency, area, and normalized-coordinate questions may additionally test rendering conventions or pixel measurement rather than the broad real-world capability claimed.

Several analyses overreach their evidence. Encoder comparisons use externally sourced checkpoints without establishing that encoder choice is the only difference; explanations involving positional embeddings are speculative. Scaling conclusions compare model variants with potentially different training data and recipes, while the cross-benchmark human-gap plot mixes heterogeneous metrics and sometimes substitutes GPT-4V for GPT-4o.

Originality is moderate rather than high. Synthetic geometry generation and basic spatial-perception diagnostics are natural extensions of prior geometry, diagram, and low-level perception benchmarks. The related-work discussion does not provide direct empirical comparisons or a careful task-overlap analysis establishing what GePBench uniquely measures.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate for a benchmark paper: code and data are only promised, and important details are missing, including generator distributions and seeds, overlap threshold, noise parameters, complete templates and distractor rules, deduplication and train-test separation procedures, caption-generation prompts, preprocessing settings, and some decoding details.

The benchmark is almost entirely synthetic and stylized, yet claims about foundational importance for medical imaging, fossils, and broad real-world applications are unsupported by transfer experiments in those domains. A clean synthetic-to-real evaluation is absent.

The limitations discussion is notably incomplete. It mentions only testing more models and enlarging an already large dataset, omitting synthetic-to-real validity, template artifacts, visual-label errors, multiple-choice biases, contamination or near-duplicate risks, uncontrolled downstream comparisons, and closed-API reproducibility.

Ethics risk is low because the benchmark is synthetic, but the human-study reporting is incomplete: five undergraduate volunteers were informed that responses would be recorded, yet compensation, recruitment safeguards, institutional oversight or exemption, and handling of recorded data are not discussed.

strengths: Significance: GePBench targets a useful and comparatively underexamined capability—basic geometric perception—and separates it into six interpretable aspects. The scale of 80K images and 285K questions could support detailed diagnostic evaluation.

Soundness: The evaluation covers 18 distinct model configurations, including strong proprietary and open models, and consistently identifies a substantial human–model gap. The per-aspect results reveal informative weaknesses, particularly for size and location.

Evidence quality: Human evaluation with five undergraduates reports 99.3% accuracy, supporting the claim that the tasks are generally understandable and solvable. The appendix also identifies exact model versions, prompts, response parsing, and training hyperparameters.

Analysis: Results stratified by shape count, noise, encoder, and resolution provide more insight than a single aggregate leaderboard. The finding that geometric performance does not reliably follow general benchmark performance is potentially valuable.

Originality and presentation: A large benchmark devoted specifically to foundational geometric perception is a useful distinction from geometry datasets centered on mathematical reasoning. The manuscript is visually polished and generally easy to follow.
Ethics: The data are procedurally generated, limiting privacy and annotation-harm concerns, and participants were informed that their responses would be recorded for academic use.
weaknesses: Soundness: The downstream-transfer experiment does not isolate geometric perception as the cause of improvement. LLaVA-GeP receives 300K additional pretraining samples and 240K additional instruction samples, but the baseline receives no size-matched generic or alternative synthetic-data control. Most gains are small, some general tasks decline, and there are no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. Consequently, the claim that the experiment demonstrates a foundational role for geometric perception is stronger than the evidence supports.

Dataset validity: The generation pipeline is insufficiently audited. Human evaluation covers only a sample, and the paper reports no automated consistency tests, ambiguity rate, inter-annotator analysis, or breakdown of human errors. Figure 1 itself contains an apparent label inconsistency: “circumscribed” is option C, while the displayed answer says “B. circumscribed.” This is concerning for a benchmark whose labels are automatically generated.

Reproducibility: Code and data are only promised for future release. Important generator details are missing, including all relationship definitions, parameter ranges, template inventories, distractor distributions, answer-position balancing, overlap threshold, random seeds, and train/test deduplication. Algorithm 1 also reuses S and R for both the supplied pools and newly initialized empty sets, making the pseudocode literally impossible to execute as written.

Evaluation design: “Easy” and “hard” jointly vary shape count and the presence of synthetic noise, confounding two sources of difficulty. The artificial noise sometimes improves accuracy, suggesting it does not reliably operationalize degradation. Exact numeric size questions may additionally test calibration to rendering coordinates rather than ordinary geometric perception; this construct choice needs stronger justification.

Ablation validity: The encoder comparison appears to use externally trained checkpoints rather than a fully controlled retraining study, so encoder identity, preprocessing, training recipe, and representation alignment may vary together. Explanations involving positional embeddings are speculative and are not directly tested.

Presentation and reporting: The manuscript repeatedly claims evaluation of 20 models, but Table 1 contains 18 model configurations. The claim of a 2.2% downstream improvement is presented without an aggregate table, variance, or a clearly defined averaging protocol, while radar plots make small differences difficult to assess.

Significance and originality: The benchmark is potentially useful, but its generator, multiple-choice templates, and LLaVA augmentation are technically straightforward. Its relationship to perception-oriented work such as BLINK and to existing synthetic geometry benchmarks needs a sharper comparison demonstrating what unique behaviors GePBench measures.

Limitations and ethics: The limitations section mentions only benchmark size and omitted models, overlooking the synthetic-to-real domain gap, template and multiple-choice shortcuts, possible label/rendering ambiguity, evaluation contamination, confounded difficulty levels, and weak causal control in the transfer experiment. Human-subject reporting does not state compensation or ethics-review/exemption status. These are addressable concerns, but the current discussion is inadequate.

Overall: The central benchmark idea and broad empirical evaluation are promising, but unresolved label-quality, reproducibility, and experimental-control issues currently prevent others from confidently building on the conclusions. Releasing the artifacts, auditing the data, and adding matched-data and multi-seed controls could move the work toward acceptance.
